utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are starting. Can the usher assist the witness? Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sekulic. [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. Sekulic, can you tell me whether you hear me well? Are your headphones working?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were discussing your testimony here and let me remind you that you should pause for a second after I have finished putting my question and then answer so that there would be no overlapping and that the interpreters could do their job well. Could you now state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Do I have to get up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. You can sit down freely while you're giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: My name is Stoko Sekulic. I was born on the 25th of October, 1947, in the village Bukovik in the municipality of Brcko. I now reside in Samac, General Draza Street, 32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me now what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I am currently retired but I worked in the Public Security Service until 1990. I was in Orasje. I started out, that is to say, as a police officer and I was the chief of the Orasje police station when I retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say public security station, you mean the police?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is the police. The police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is Orasje a municipality neighbouring the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is some 20 kilometres away from the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I served the Yugoslav People's Army in 1966, 1967. I was in the school for reserve officers traffic specialty unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, are you married?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married with two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I was informed that your rank did not enter the record, when you said that you completed the reserve military officers school and you graduated with the rank of...?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: A second lieutenant, when I finished the military service, and completed the school, I ended up as the junior lieutenant and that is in the traffic specialty unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me now whether you were a member of a political party? Are you a member of a political party now?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists since -- I have been since 1962. This was up until the war, and then ever since the war period, I haven't been a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, before the outbreak of the hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell us where you resided?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, since 1981, I was in the Public Security Service I lived in Orasje up to 1990. I continued living there. I had a socially owned flat and in 1992 on the 8th of March, I left Orasje and went to Bac where I remained until the 13th [as interpreted] of April, 1992, when I went to Bosanski Samac or to be precise, to Obudovac, because my wife is from Obudovac, she has a house there and her parents have a house and that is where I started -- residing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. What was the reason for your departure from Orasje to Bac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I left Orasje for Bac because I had a colleague who needed a worker to drive his truck and that is what I did. I worked until the 13th [as interpreted] of April in Bac and I was staying at the hotel central in Bac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have one correction for the transcript. The witness was always referring to the 30th of April and here we see 13th of April on page 3, line --

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And also on page 4, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The 30th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of April, 3-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That will be corrected. 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where is Bac situated in relation to Bosanski Samac, in relation to Orasje?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, it is -- it was situated in the then Yugoslavia. Bac is a larger town. It is close to Banatska Palanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is in Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes in Vojvodina, the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let us talk now about a specific date, the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Can you tell us where exactly were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: On the 16th and 17th of April, I was in Bac because I was there until the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how did it come about that you started working in the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, on the 30th of April, I arrived in Obudovac and the following day, that is on the 1st of May of 1992, I went to the department for Defence which is where I found someone, I'm not sure if his name is Bogdanovic, Milos, but because I hadn't been living there before he was the head of the Defence department, and so I reported there. I actually wanted to register myself because I had arrived from a different municipality to the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and then Milos referred me to the police station, which was at the time called Bosanski Samac police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So where was it exactly that you reported to the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1992, around noon, 1.00 p.m., I'm not definite about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who you reported to in the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: In the police station, I reported to Mr. Stevan Todorovic, who was then Chief of Police in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period between 1st of May, 1992, onwards, when you met Stevan Todorovic, which tasks were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the duties of a police officer or a militia worker as it was called at the time, and it was immediately on the 1st of May that I was referred to the Defence line in Grebnica. This was the village of Grebnica where the Defence line was at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To define all the duties that you discharged in the police, one of these duties was then to go to the Defence line with the other policemen to hold the line there in Grebnica. Can you tell us which were the other tasks you discharged during your service for the police?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: While I was working for the police, when I arrived to this particular municipality, I would also provide security for the post office, for instance, for the social company of Master [Realtime transcript read in error "Matter"], of waterworks and a high school as well, where some people were kept in isolation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will just put two more brief questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A small correction in the transcript, on page 6, line 4, company is Master. We already referred to this company in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever provide security for the building of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever provide security for the gym hall of the elementary school in Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you worked providing security for the high school only for two days?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, two shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While discharging these duties, did you ever take part in the -- in arresting people and bringing them over to the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in the process of taking people into custody in the police station, not me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question in regard to this: Did you ever take part in the searching of flats of certain persons in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, these duties that you mentioned, were they -- did they require you to stay in the police station building or did they actually require you to spend most of the time outside the building?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the time I was outside the building and most of the time I actually spent on the Defence line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, at one point you became deputy commander of the police station. Can you tell me when this happened and how come?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, in the morning, I came from the area of Grebnica to Samac, and I was sleeping in the hotel upstairs, and some offices and a colleague was there too. I had come from the shift around 6.20 and I just washed up a bit and went to bed and soon after that, Slobodan Jovanovic, a police officer, came and told me to report to the Chief of Police, the chief of SUP, at his office. I got up, got ready, went to the chief and then the chief told me that he's appointing me the deputy commander of the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can I ask you one question and then we can move on. Before you, who was deputy commander at the police station, before you got this position?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Before me, it was Mr. Milan Jekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please continue now? So you came to the Chief of Police and what did he say to you and what did you say?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that the chief said that he was appointing me deputy commander of the police station in Samac and I refused that. I refused that because I thought that there were people who were from that area, from that town. I did not know the area. I did not know Samac. I never worked there. But he kept on insisting, and finally, I stayed there until 9.00 and then went back to the hotel to get some more sleep and then around 12.00, Slobodan Jovanovic came again, and then again I went to the department store to the office of the Chief of Police, which is where he told me that I had to accept this position because Mr. Jekic no longer wanted to do that work, and then I accepted the job. I accepted it for the following reasons. Well, how can I put this? I was sort of afraid of some individuals because during my work, I saw that there were people who had come from Serbia and we were not or rather I was not in any kind of close relations with them and I sort of avoided them and then I accepted this ultimately. I was afraid for my own sake. I accepted this. Immediately, I spoke to Mr. Todorovic, the Chief of Police, about certain matters because I said that I would accept the job on the condition that the law on the interior is applied and according to the rules of service of the security services, and also, the by-laws, all the other by-laws that were relevant to the MUP of Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Until now, it was not contested before this Tribunal that there was a rather large number of people who were detained at the TO and at the SUP building and that the conditions under which they were detained were rather poor. Can you tell us about your experience? What the conditions were, the detention conditions of those people who were at the TO and at the SUP, who were detained there at the time?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: As a public security official, I mean I worked there from 1981 and I knew what the conditions were supposed to be in prisons generally speaking if we are talking about prisons but in this case, this was isolation. These conditions were really bad. But they were not so bad because somebody wanted them to be that bad. It was simply due to the prevalent material conditions at the time. Better conditions could not be provided. When I came, I agreed with the Chief of Police that -- and he actually told me that I should do my best, and that I should do as I see fit, and I said that I think that the law on the interior should be applied and the rules of service and public security and the relevant by-laws and I saw that these people who had already been isolated there, I saw that they were not taking baths, that they were not changing their clothes, and I agreed then with Slobodan Jovanovic, who at that time was working in finance, well, perhaps this is primitive but this is what the situation was and there was no other way of working then because there wasn't even electricity or water then. Any way, we prepared the following. I mean, in these facilities, there weren't any bathrooms or anything, so we organised some taps there, we needed tap water for these people. It was summertime so these people could at least take baths once a week but twice a week we allowed the families of these people to bring them a change of clothes. So personal hygiene could be maintained at least up to a degree, as far as these people were concerned. I mean within the scope of our possibilities, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Mr. Sekulic. Could you just speak a bit slower? Everything should be recorded the way you have put it and it needs to be interpreted. Did you have any problems with these specials from Serbia, these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, since I did not even meet these people when they came, I don't even know when they came but then when I came I had some problems quite specific problems with Lugar, I don't know, I don't know what his real name is. I didn't really have any problems with others within the service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now I am just going to put a few more questions to you. You know Simo Zaric, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No, I know Simo Zaric from before. He worked in the public security while I worked there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you worked at the police station from the 1st of May onwards, while you were employed in the Public Security Service, did you ever see Simo Zaric at the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you now from the 1st of May, 1992, until the end of the war, I saw Simo Zaric perhaps two or three times in Samac, in town, in passing, I never saw him at the police station itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was Simo Zaric perhaps a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of May, I never saw him as one over there. I mean, from the 1st of May onwards, no. I don't know about before the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions that have to do with the arrival of the International Red Cross in Samac and their visit to detainees. Tell me, did the International Red Cross come to visit detainees in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. I cannot remember the date but I can say that this is the period either -- well, I don't know, from the end of August, the end of August, the beginning of September, or the end of September, and the beginning of November [as interpreted]. Well, any way, a delegation came consisting of two members, and there was a third person, an interpreter. There was a man there, I can describe him because in my diary, I wrote it down, I haven't got that diary any more, the man was about 28, the woman was about 20 and then there was the interpreter too, and they came to my office, we had a cup of coffee, we went out. I cannot give you the time now. I can -- a shell came from the area of Croatia. It hit a garage. It killed Vukovic. I think his name was Vukovic. He was in isolation and he was sitting in front and drinking coffee and this shell killed him. So then when they got out of the office, we went to the garage, we were right there in front of the garage where that happened so they saw that and then we went back to the building and then we went to the TO staff where people were in isolation. They probably intended to talk. I mean they saw the conditions under which these people lived. They wanted to see the rooms where these people were isolated. However, we didn't cross the street halfway when the shelling started. These three members of the delegation, they lay on the pavement but I just remained standing because this was not the first time the shells started falling on Orasje, no not Orasje, Samac, and then after that, they got up and then this member of this delegation asked me, what's this? And I said, "Our brothers have sent us a present. A present from the Republic of Croatia." And then he asked me whether this was a frequent occurrence and I said a frequent occurrence indeed, almost every day -- every night, there were shells falling all over Samac and then we went to the TO staff where people were put up, people who were in isolation. They just went through the premises, they saw what they looked like and then they got out and they did not return to my office, they immediately went into the land rover which had a sign of the Red Cross on and then they left in a direction unknown to me. Well, I'm not sure. As for the local authorities, whether Mr. Milan Simic was with them. I think that he came with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, now I am interested in Simo Zaric specifically. When the members, the representatives of the International Red Cross were present, was Mr. Zaric ever present there together with you, or did you perhaps see him on his own?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Simo was never there with me. When I spoke a while ago, I said that I never saw Simo Zaric, not at all, in the building or at the TO staff. I saw Simo Zaric in the street. I've already said that. Perhaps two or three times during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me how long you stayed at the police in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Until the 31st of August, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any other questions from counsel? The Prosecution, cross-examination? Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sekulic, my name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to ask you some questions this morning. Now, sir, you said that the conditions were really bad at the police station and you said it was due to the prevalent conditions this morning. The prevalent conditions in the town, the bombing the lack of water, the lack of electricity, isn't that correct? That's what you testified this morning.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, sir, the beatings, the rape of prisoners, the murders that occurred there, those weren't the result of the prevalent conditions in the town, were they?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, probably not, but I did not see that. I'm not aware of that. I really did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is uncontested in this case that torture -- that prisoners were tortured, beaten on a daily basis, that they had their teeth extracted at the police station and across the street at the TO. Those were not the result of the prevalent conditions in the town, the lack of water, the shelling, the poor electricity. Those incidents could not be the result of the prevalent conditions in the town.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Of course they could not, but I could just say that from the 3rd of August onwards, the 3rd of August, 1992, that there were no more such cases. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was very kind of you but prior to your being named the deputy, the conditions there were very poor. In fact, your supervisor or police chief was Stevan Todorovic, isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware that Stevan Todorovic has pled guilty to the persecution of the non-Serb civilians in Bosanski Samac. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of some of the things I read about in the newspapers, the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, were you aware that Stevan Todorovic has admitted to the cruel and inhumane treatment of the non-Serb civilians including confining them in inhumane conditions at the TO, the Territorial Defence building, the police station, the primary school and the secondary school? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I have already said here that for the most part, I was in the field and dealing with facilities. I just read about this in the newspapers. I read about Stevan et cetera. I never heard of anybody mistreating anybody. You've just referred to teeth extraction. I never heard [as interpreted] of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware that prior to your coming there and after your coming there, to Bosanski Samac, almost 200 teeth were extracted from prisoners at the TO, at the SUP, and at the primary school? You weren't aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, there is one just small correction for the transcript. Maybe it would explain. When the witness was answering to Prosecutor questions on page 14, line 14 and 15, he said I never saw of any of such things, not I never heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not blaming you for those, sir, I'm not blaming you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can ask him to clarify because he's the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is that you never saw these things occur in your presence, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did not see that and this did not happen in my presence. Now what I heard was something different. It's different if you experience something and see something and it's different if you hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do admit that the conditions were poor during the summer of 1992 at the TO? I'm sorry, at the police station.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I admit because since I worked there I know what kind of conditions existed in prisons. I was even aware of some excerpts from the Geneva Conventions, as far as prisoners are concerned. That is why I took the kind of action that I took and as I said, to improve personal hygiene, whatever the social political community can do, improve the food a bit. The food was the way it was, depending on the conditions that prevailed in the social political community. The army did not have better food, any food that was better than what the detainees had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you examine at the primary school the portions that they were receiving? The portions of food at the primary school.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: The food for the primary school and for the TO staff was the same, two meals during the course of the day. I saw that when it was brought from Tekstilac. Food was brought from Tekstilac, from this one kitchen where we all got our meals from. We all had our meals at Tekstilac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them distributing the food to the prisoners at the TO? And at the primary school? Because those people have testified and it's been uncontested in this case that they were only receiving one meal a day.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I know that two meals were taken, when I came, two meals were taken from Tekstilac. I saw that for sure. They put it in the appropriate dishes and took it to the TO staff and to the school et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... questioning but if we could have a time frame for this maybe it would assist in that way we would be fair to the witness, whether it was prior, he became assistant commander or after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the spring, plus June and July, the testimony here has been uncontested that the prisoners were receiving one meal a day for a short time in April they received two. But they were only receiving one meal a day. Now, sir, they might have been receiving it at the facility, two meals, but the prisoners, the testimony has been that the prisoners themselves only received one meal. Were you present when two meals were given to each prisoner at the Territorial Defence building, or the primary school? Or the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Look, I have to make a reservation here. For instance, I know well that I was sitting at the high school centre. There was a weeping willow there and there were employees of the police whom I knew, like Filip, Marko, head of the criminal investigations section, and I can't remember all the names of the people I knew. Any way, my father-in-law and my wife came and brought me food. I shared it with them, and on that occasion, I heard from Filip, it was in the month of May, that they were receiving two meals. I never saw it with my own eyes. I wasn't the quartermaster, I didn't go to the Tekstilac company to bring the food back to this facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Let's move on a little bit. You indicated that when you first joined the police department they sent you to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Right on the 1st of May, in the evening, I was already at Grebnica, because we were holding the defence line there. We were one platoon of the police holding one stretch of that line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: From the side of Orasje and Domaljevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you said you were one platoon of police officers. How many police officers constitute one platoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Up to 30 police, 28 to 30 policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there military -- members of the military, or JNA, also there?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, this police platoon, I have to go back to the name of militia because in 1992 it was called the militia, not the police. This militia platoon was under the authority of what I think was called the 5th Battalion, and we were carrying out the defence tasks given us by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say 5th Battalion, are you referring to the JNA's 4th Detachment which was the detachment in Samac? Is that what you're referring to? Or was this --

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, this 4th Detachment had grown into the 5th Battalion. I must say I don't know much about this but I think it was later called the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this was -- you indicated you were under the direction of this 5th Battalion and that's part of the JNA, isn't that correct? And then later became part of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that this might lead this witness to some misconclusions because 5th Battalion was a battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska so just let's not make things that it was at any point the 5th Battalion was a part of JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, Your Honour, on May 1, there was no Army of Republika Srpska. So he has to be talking -- whatever unit he's talking about he has to be talking about a JNA unit that was later converted into the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness should know what he's talking about. So if he doesn't understand or doesn't know anything, he should say so, so he's able to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was this battalion part of the military whether it was the JNA or the Army of Republika Srpska? Was it part of the military?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was part of the army and I can't remember the exact date now when it got the name of the Army of Republika Srpska. I really can't remember the date because I wasn't serving in the army at the time. I was serving in the militia, and I believe that this 5th Battalion or the 4th Detachment, as it was called at the beginning, at the beginning of the war, I mentioned the 5th Battalion because that's what stuck in my mind when I was leaving for those defence lines, at that time it was already called the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. No problem. It's 11 years ago so, almost 11 years ago so I understand you might not always be sure of the exact names or dates. Now, you indicate, sir -- let's move on because we have very limited time, our cross-examination has been restricted in time today so I want to get to one more subject, sir. You indicated that you became the deputy commander on or about August 3rd, 1992 and that sometime after that you were visited by the Red Cross on two or three occasions and this is the International Red Cross, you met with them on two or through occasions?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: No. I only once met with the delegation of the International Red Cross, only once, and I told you about that day. I don't know the exact date or time when they visited but it was only that one time, as I said before. On that day, as I mentioned, there was shelling, and maybe that delegation would have stayed longer had it not been for the shelling. As it was, they just passed through briefly, viewed the conditions and left. They were probably afraid of the shelling and couldn't wait to get out of that hell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Red Cross had come on some other occasions that you had not met them, when you had not met them, at the police station?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware because nobody informed me. Who was I to be informed that a delegation of the International Red Cross was coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that one occasion you met them. Let's go through that incident. You don't recall the exact date. You know it is in some period in the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're not aware of the exact time that they came to Samac?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, I've told you before, I mentioned three possibilities, beginning of August, end of September, or beginning of October. I can't decide exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm saying you're not aware of the exact time. You can't say that they came at 10.00 or 10.30 or 11.15, you're not aware of the exact date and you're not aware of the exact time.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I know about that. It was not at 10.00 or even 12.00. This was in the afternoon. It could only have been after 1.00 p.m. when they came to my office with Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't know the names of the person who came to visit you?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: At that time, I had my agenda and I wrote down the name of the man and the name of the interpreter and I could even describe them now. He was about 28 years old, he was about 180 centimetres tall, but I can't tell you now his name, 11 years passed since. I don't remember what I had for lunch yesterday let alone this man's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's right. You don't have your diary any more, you have no records, you have no documents, so you're basically going off of your memory at this point. It's 11 years since this incident has happened.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm only relying on my memory. I have no records. I used to have that agenda but I don't have it any more and I can't really know who visited. I don't remember the names of the people or the interpreter and the second member of the delegation who was a woman. How am I supposed to remember? It was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to that, had you been inside the TO facility, the TO, the warehouses, the yard, and gone through the whole area? Prior to that visit?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I passed through, I told you before, and when I assumed my duties of deputy commander, when I first came into the premises, I saw that it was awfully dirty, hygiene was very poor, I realised something had to be done, and something was done, to the extent of our possibilities. That means cleaning the rooms, airing the rooms, providing change of clothes for the people. I saw what could be done to redress the situation and that was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Red Cross came they stayed only a short time because of the bombing, isn't that correct? The shelling. They stayed a very short time, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, they only passed through the rooms, and I'm telling you my opinion now. It is not necessarily true, only the head of that delegation could tell you for sure. They only passed through, viewed the rooms where the people were isolated, and went straight out. They said goodbye to me got into their land rover and went off, I don't know where. In terms of time, it wasn't more than two or three minutes they spent viewing the rooms before they got into their car and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that they went into the staff building. That's the first building in the TO, they walked right into that first building or office. Did they go into the courtyard? Did they go into the warehouse, the rooms inside of the warehouse? Did they also visit those? First, were you with them? Did you accompany them into those rooms?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I already told you I was with them the whole time from the time they came into my office, and we went together to the SUP and came back, when this shelling happened, from the street, you go directly into the TO headquarters, TO staff building, and it was within the compound of the SUP that they saw the barrels in which people took baths, and after that they went to the warehouse. As far as I know it is still a warehouse. It was in that warehouse that those pallets were where people lay. They spent altogether two or three minutes there, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, and sir you have no records at this point in relation to that day, you have no diary, no records in relation to that incident, isn't that correct, in relation to that visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we already have the answer to this question. It was -- I mean, I see no reason why asking two times the very same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Time frame for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has already explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that prisoners were isolated at the high school, isn't that correct? You testified today that prisoners were isolated, that people were isolated at the high school when you first arrived sometime in May. You visited the high school and saw people there that were isolated. And sir, the people that were isolated, do you know of what ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I know they were both Croats and Muslims and I just told you there were colleagues with whom I used to sit down for a drink. We were colleagues even before the war. We had known each other. And I mentioned this occasion when my father-in-law and my wife came bringing me food and I shared it with them under that weeping willow. Whenever I had cigarettes, I shared them. I treated them as human beings, just as they treated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the people that were isolated at the Territorial Defence building, those were also Muslims and Croats, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that were isolated at the primary school or held at the primary school, those were also Muslims and Croats, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in the Balkans, you had those unfortunate isolation centres, and of course people were taken into custody for certain reasons, such as for the purpose of conducting so-called informative interviews, and it was the same in all areas of the former Yugoslavia whether populated by Muslims, Croats or Serbs, wherever the army held --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir but the people in Bosanski Samac that were isolated or being held, those as you called them, those unfortunate -- in those unfortunate isolation centres, those were Muslims and Croats, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Well, we all know that, that they were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one very brief matter. Re-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sekulic, you said during your testimony and this was later picked up by the Prosecutor, namely that your platoon was sent to Grebnica to hold the line there. Do you remember the Prosecutor asking you that? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, you said that while you were there, holding the defence line, you were under the command of the army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back to Bosanski Samac after those military operations, under whose command would you then be?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: Whenever we came back to Samac, we went back to our work under the command of the MUP, that is our chief of the police. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. Sekulic. I just have a couple of questions for you concerning the visit that you've been discussing of the International Committee of the Red Cross to Samac. What I would like to know was whether the International Committee of the Red Cross delegation, these two people that you mentioned, whether they asked you when they were having coffee in your office whether they could talk to any of the detained persons in either the SUP or the TO or the schools.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: They absolutely never asked me to have an interview with anyone. If they had asked for it, I would have made sure they could do it, because as soon as we went off to the TO staff, I thought we were going there in order for them to talk to people who were in isolation. And I really thought about that day when this shelling happened that they had lost their nerve and they couldn't wait to get out. So no, the answer is no, nobody asked me about that, and I did think they might want to talk to the people who were in isolation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The second question is: At the TO, you say they went to the warehouse. I'm interested to know whether the cells which were those little garages in the yard, whether it was pointed out to them that persons were kept in those small set of garages, and so whether they knew and whether they wanted to go and look inside. Maybe you could just say a few words on that.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know the extent that you know about these small garages but I do claim that in the TO building, these were large garages and there was a warehouse, the warehouse was also pretty large, and people slept on the pallets and they had blankets to the extent that they had, and there was also the attic, and this was all very easily accessible. It was large. These were no small garages. These were large rooms. The only thing was that they housed a large number of people with the blankets on the pallets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can be of some assistance. The garages were in the yard of the SUP, not in the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There were also garages at the TO, in the courtyard, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. The last questions are very short. I'm just wondering whether they had the opportunity to see any of the food that was to be distributed to the detained persons, and also whether they asked anything about the meals.

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: The -- this particular gentleman and the lady who was with him, they did not ask me about the food at all, at least I wasn't asked about the food. They were with the representatives of the local authorities, they were probably taken into the kitchens where the food was being prepared but this is something I know nothing of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And lastly, when they did tour the premises of the SUP and the TO, were they taken to see the toilet and shower facilities for the detained persons?

utterances.speaker: STOKO SEKULIC
utterances.text: They were able to see the showers because the showers were on the roof [as interpreted], they were exposed to the sun, in order for the water to be heated. This is what they saw. There was one toilet there which they saw, over there in the building, and I'm sure that they did see that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one small correction. It was misinterpreted here. Here it says on page 26, line 18, that the showers were on the roof, and this is actually not what the witness said. They were not on the roof. They were in the yards, in the circle, the way he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the compound of the yard, in the yard itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Sekulic. We are finished with your evidence. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Before the next witness is brought in, I believe Mr. Arnautovic, there is just a very brief matter I need to raise with you concerning that witness. Late yesterday afternoon, the Prosecution received the search materials relating to this witness. Last night, as I was preparing for this witness, I came across a statement that this witness has made to the OTP. I notified the Defence this morning of the existence of that statement. I'm happy to say that the statement was disclosed on the 23rd of November, 1999. The statement is in English. I've got copies of the statement here and I'm prepared obviously prepared to provide that to the Defence. They haven't yet had an opportunity to read the statement or take any instructions that they might want to take from the witness or raise issues with the witness that are contained in the statement. I don't know, of course, if I'm going to use the statement in cross-examination or not. It may be that I won't have to use it. I don't know. I can't predict, as I don't have any sort of summary of what the witness is going to say. But just as a matter of courtesy to the Defence I thought I ought -- and to the bench, I ought to raise this with you and as far as the Prosecution is concerned, I'm in a position now to hand copies of the statement to Defence counsel and the Prosecution would not oppose a short adjournment if they need it to raise with the next witness any matters contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm surprised that the Prosecution doesn't have a summary of what this witness is going to discuss because the summaries were filed -- MR. DI FAZIO: There is what I've seen is about four lines. I know the topic that the witness is going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The 18th or something but I don't actually have a -- I can make an educated guess as to what he's going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No these summaries were filed in November last year and these are the witnesses which the Trial Chamber moved from depositions and he's supposed to discuss the collection of weaponry in Pere Bosica Street, the isolated incident involving Mr. Zaric. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In front of Esad and Safet Dagovic's house mentioned as neighbour. This is dealing with paragraph 15 of the indictment, and he's scheduled to give evidence in half an hour. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. I've got no complaint with the witness coming right in now. All I'm say something is I've got this statement and I believe that the Defence have not seen it and all I'm saying is that I'm just letting all the parties the Chamber become aware of that and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And say that here it is, if you want sometime the Prosecution has no objection to an adjournment for a brief period of time to enable the Defence to speak to the witness. I'm trying to avoid any suggestion of ambush or any unfairness on the part of the Prosecution. That's all I'm driving at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Can the witness be brought in, please? MR. DI FAZIO: May I just cross the courtroom and provide a copy nonetheless to the defence if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The copy of the statement, Mr. Di Fazio, is the one which was already disclosed in 1999, isn't it? MR. DI FAZIO: I believe so, from what my case manager has told me this morning, he's done his researches. There may be a B/C/S translation of the document that I don't have with me here but the statement is in English. The signed one is in English. And there is the acknowledgement at the end of it with the interpreter and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: So that is the actual statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask copies to be distributed for the other Defence teams as well of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was it given only to one party? MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I do apologise. Yes, I can do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes, can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear so well, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you increase the volume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If maybe the volume could be increased? My hearing is impaired. My hearing is impaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can hear me then?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I spoke to you, we discussed a bit the technical aspect of your testimony. I will just now remind you to pause a bit, a few seconds, after I have put my question to you and then start with your answer, the goal being that your testimony is put into the record the way you have said it. Could you state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: 9th of March, 1931.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you were born?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Trebinje, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trebinje is in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. First it was Herzegovina, well it is Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina but in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: High-skilled machinist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your status is at present? Are you a pensioner?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I have been retired since 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the army in 1951 and 1952, in Belgrade, in Tito's guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists until 1972, and I haven't been a member ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you have not been a member of any political party since?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have never declared myself to be either this or that to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where did you reside in 1992? Did you live in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in Pere Bosica Street?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, formerly Pere Bosica Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still live there today?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which house is -- stands on the opposite -- opposite to your house in Pere Bosica Street and who does it belong to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: The house across from where my house is is the house of Sulejman and Sabrija Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are these actually two houses, one is the house of Sulejman Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is his house and Sabrija's house is a separate one and it is a bit behind Sulejman's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are two houses actually?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you know the families Dagovic well, both the family of Sulejman Dagovic and Sabrija Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I have known them for 30, 31 years, I also helped them build their house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the fact that -- do you know if Sabrija Dagovic has children?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She [as interpreted] has two sons, Esad Dagovic and Safet Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Small correction, here it says she has two sons. Sabrija is a male, not a female. So he has two sons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a wife?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your wife with you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this 17th of April, 1992, so on that morning, what did you see on the 17th of April? Were there any armed civilians who were fleeing towards the bridge on the Bosna River and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I did see, there were these parties, the SDA, the SDS, so how could I know? At that time there were these parties that were ruling, and there were about 30 or 40 of these paramilitary formations of the SDA in Samac with light weapons and I saw some people who were fleeing to the neighbouring village, with weapons, across the Bosna River. This village is Prud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall any of the people you recognised on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Udzvalic, I don't know his first name. I know his father's name is Mustafa. So it is Mustafa Udzvalic's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that day on the 17th did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend the night there between the 17th and the 18th? Were you asleep?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally and your family have any problems?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of correcting the transcript, page 34, line 2, it says that armed formations of the SDS were fleeing to Prud. Could my colleague, Mr. Pisarevic, check this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is not what it says in transcript. It says paramilitary formation of the SDA. This is what it says on page 34, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in second line he says SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just take the witness back so that he can give the correct answer, if he can speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just speak a bit more distinctly and slower so the people could understand you? Members of this paramilitary formation, who did they actually belong to, these people who were fleeing to the village of Prud?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: This paramilitary formation was not the regular army. They were a civilian organisation armed by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Arnautovic, this was just for the purposes of the transcript to have this clarified a bit. Now we've moved on to another day, that is the 18th of April. What did you see on that day from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request could the witness's microphone please be turned on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the 4th Detachment, were they collecting weapons and what did you see on that day and who? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Fadil Topcagic and a colleague of his, they were walking towards the house where they knew that the people had weapons, that is Esad Dagovic and Safet Dagovic. The two of them went to the house and asked for the weapons that I saw later. They took it out later. A Kalashnikov and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you saw this. Were there any other persons in military uniform with Fadil and with this other person who you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: This was somewhat later. This was the second or the third day when they were entering the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. We are talking about the 18th, the 18th only. With Fadil and with this other person, were there any other members of the 4th Detachment in uniform and did anybody come to you, to your house? Did anybody knock at the door of your house and ask for weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had set out towards my house but this neighbour, how should I call him, Fadil, said that there was no one here at the house because they were elderly people, they had no weapons, he said that they are pensioners there and there is nothing to be looked for over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And these soldiers were in the same group with Fadil, they did not come to you at all?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that it wasn't only Fadil and this one man but that there was a group of soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group of soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you entered the house. Did you see them enter the yard? Where did they go? Who went out, et cetera? Did you see this contact, what it actually looked like? Did they first knock at Sulejman's door and did they then go to Sabrija Dagovic's house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Dagovic, Sulejman, his house faces the road, whereas Sabrija's house is in the backyard and there was no one else by Sulejman at the house because he worked at the hospital. Dagovic, Sabrija was at home with his wife and his children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see when Fadil and two other soldiers walked into the yard and went to the house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether they entered the house or not?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: They did not enter the house. They knocked at the door. They came out and asked to take the weapons out, the weapons they had. They first took out the Kalashnikov. They knew that there were other weapons, the young boy brought the pistol too, brought it out later. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this witness is ascribing all sorts of knowledge and conversation that he can hear. There is absolutely no basis for this. You haven't heard, we don't know, he might have been peeking out of his window through his curtains looking at these events. If so, how could he hear the conversation or he might have strolled across the road and had been present, we don't know. There is no foundation for him to make these assertions and he's also talking about the knowledge of Fadil Topcagic, some basis has to be established for how he can say what was in Fadil's Topcagic's mind, how he knows what Fadil Topcagic knew. Otherwise this evidence is worthless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you understood the points made by Mr. Di Fazio, so you can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes, Your Honours. This is all quite clear to me. I'm going to ask the witness precisely now whether he saw it and from which place he saw it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it and I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you saw it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it because my house has an upstairs floor and his house is nearby and I saw the yard where he walked in and I heard him asking for weapons and I heard him ask the children to bring out the weapons, and I saw him when he brought the weapons out of the house and we handed in both one and the other because it's not far away. It's 15 metres only. I heard this a bit better now so yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you watched all of this from the window of your house and that window is upstairs on the first floor of your house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that this would be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break and continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arnautovic, before the break we discussed the place from which you observed all this -- all these events that were occurring in the street, and in the Dagovic yard. Tell me, please, what else did you see on that occasion? Did you see anyone else accompanying those members of the 4th Detachment, perhaps a vehicle or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see a vehicle that was coming from the direction of the Bosna and Sava Rivers towards my street, Pere Bosica Street. It was a sort of anti-aircraft, self-propelled thing. This vehicle turned towards the village of Tisina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Simo Zaric well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see Mr. Simo Zaric, together with those soldiers, outside your house and the Dagovic house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't. Simo Zaric was not on top of that vehicle and I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I do, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What happened after a couple of months when an airplane bombed the city of -- sorry, the town of Samac? What happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of September, at 1900 hours, or rather 2120 hours, we heard the sound of an engine that resembled the sound of a tractor. I was in the basement of my house and I wanted to come out of the house but my wife didn't allow it, and then we heard an explosion, a bomb from that airplane fell on the city waterworks and another bomb fell on my house. A third bomb fell into the yard of the neighbour's house. The neighbour's name was Ovijeta Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your house damaged on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't damaged. It was almost demolished. It was a terribly loud explosion. That bomb was about ten to 15 kilos of explosive. You can imagine what kind of detonation that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who came to your house offering help?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: That evening, at 9.25, and I must say I am beside myself with joy because I stayed alive, troops came to my house offering help, Dr. Ozren asked me if anyone was hurt. I said nobody was hurt and he said, "That's impossible. The house is almost demolished." We crossed the yard to go to the shelter across the street, and the next morning, I went to inspect the damage. I went into the house. I saw only ruins and rubble. Nothing was left intact. And the first person who came to see me after that was Miroslav Tadic. He offered assistance, saying, don't worry, everything will be all right. Don't worry, the main thing is that you're alive and well. He was the first one who came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was Miroslav Tadic who came, that it wasn't Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, so sorry, it was Simo Zaric of course. He was the first one who came. The first person who offered me a kind word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, any other counsel? Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, Serbian paramilitaries took over the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that that was accompanied by the declaration of a Serbian Crisis Staff and that took over the civilian administration of the town?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the activities of those paramilitaries, either on the night of the 16th and 17th, or on the 17th of April? Did you see what they were up to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those paramilitary formations that had come from outside, whether it was from Belgrade or some other place, I don't know, they harassed people, they came into their houses, looking for things that they wanted to take, such as money, valuables, jewellery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly I don't disagree with you that they were doing that but do you agree with me that one of the things that they were doing was going around to houses and seizing weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many people had any weapons in their houses. There was not much weaponry in Samac and it was the 4th Detachment that collected those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we certainly don't disagree on that point, Mr. Arnautovic. However, my question was: Did you see paramilitaries going into houses, maybe doing all sorts of other things, but also seizing weapons from the people, the citizenry of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did see, and they came into my neighbour's house, took jewellery off their wrists and necklaces from their necks, and as far as weapons are concerned, there was very few of that in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it your position then that you did not see paramilitaries take or seize weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of that happening, paramilitaries seizing weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, there were no weapons in Samac. If there were any, there were very few because they had already been turned over to the 4th Corps, the 4th Corps had already collected the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, the people who had weapons had already run away from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paramilitaries came in on the night of the 16th and 17th. They came into the town. There were bombs, explosions and shooting, correct? Just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the paramilitaries were carrying out activities on the day of the 17th, correct? Just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the 17th, when those paramilitaries were carrying out their activities are you aware in any what whatsoever of them seizing weapons? That's all I want to know. Not jewellery, not property, not doing bad things, just focus on that one issue. Are you aware of paramilitaries seizing weapons on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has already answered twice that he is not aware that paramilitary formations rounded up weapons around Samac. He said that the 4th Detachment did that and the Prosecutor is asking the question for the third and the fourth time already, although he already has an answer. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. I'll withdraw the question and proceed to the events of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, did you see -- I'm sorry, the 18th of April. On that day, you saw the soldiers go to [Realtime transcript read in error "into"] the house of the Dagovic family and they were members of the 4th Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. Paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, the witness didn't say they went into the house. He said they went into the yards and the members of the 4th Detachment never went into a house. Please don't confuse the witness by asking such questions. If you want to ask a question, don't phrase it as if he had said it that way. Please ask fair questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic, but I think there is just a misunderstanding here. Mr. Di Fazio in his question, page 43, line 8, did not say you saw the soldiers go into the house. He said you saw the soldiers go to the house. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And witness, that's exactly what I meant. On that day, the 18th of April, you saw members of the 4th Detachment go to the house. I'm not saying they went inside the house but they went to the house, stood outside the house. That's correct, right? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many were they?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the people who came outside the house? There were two of them from the 4th Detachment. They were looking for weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they accompanied by a larger group of 4th Detachment soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've testified to seeing a vehicle this morning, let me rephrase that. This morning in court you have testified that you saw a vehicle. That was on the 18th and that was at about the time that the soldiers went to the house of Esad Dagovic, a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't go to Dagovic's house in that military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away was the military vehicle from the house of Esad Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, ten, maybe 12 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And surrounding that vehicle, were there soldiers from the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the entire collection of people out in the street in front of the house were two soldiers from the 4th Detachment and one military vehicle? That's it? No other people?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. That vehicle set off and went on its way without stopping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But the -- so it never stopped, it just passed by the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a tank?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was this self-propelled thing with one machine-gun or whatever it was, maybe a light cannon. It wasn't a tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
