That's not against Dr. Blagoje Simic. It's against the witness. They are different purposes. And in relation to the disclosure I was saying that Mr. Pantelic lead council has had the statement since 1999 and Mr. Pantelic was in fact the person who provided us with this witness's witness statement which was given to Mr. Pisarevic. Our records show Mr. Pantelic, lead counsel for Dr. Simic provided the Prosecution with Mr. Omeranovic's statement to Mr. Pisarevic taken in 1996. The lawyers for Dr. Blagoje Simic have had these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re, the point is Dr. Blagoje Simic was not on this case and the Trial Chamber is going to allow you to use the statement only in relation to Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour that was all I wanted to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, you made the statement in 1998 and when you made the statement, you -- it was read to you in the Croatian language by the interpreter, Ms. Irena Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, just a brief remark, if you allow, if Dr. Blagoje Simic is not mentioned in the statement, this does not mean that it cannot prejudice his case. If the SDS party is mentioned or something else. So the Prosecutor should be able to use the statement but not regarding those circumstances that could be prejudicial to Dr. Blagoje Simic, relating to SDS or any other issue related to the accused in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought the issue in the trial was not that the SDS had done things but that Dr. Simic had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I've already said that the statement will be used only in relation to Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not arguing. Mr. Vukovic keeps popping up and down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the third time Mr. Omeranovic, the statement which you signed in 1998 was read over to you by an interpreter, Ms. Martinovic, in the Croatian language and as a result of her reading it to you, you signed each page of the English version as it being correct, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this was no statement. This was merely an interview. I personally came to this interview. It was just an interview. There was no statement there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two interviewers, two investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor, that's Mr. Selsky and Mr. Roy, that's the French-Canadian gentlemen, both Canadians, came and spoke to you about the events during the war, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: We talked, since I lived in Belgium for a while, and actually 20 years later, I wanted to refresh the knowledge of my language, I knew that he was Canadian and we started speaking French and he asked me things about family, privates, so it was just merely more a sort of an informal talk. We actually spent more time talking about these things rather than those others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeranovic, you -- the languages spoken in this conversation were French, Serbian, Bosnian, Croatian, but not new Croatian. Those were the languages you spoke with Mr. Selsky, Mr. Roy, and Ms. Martinovic, weren't they? French, Serbian, Bosnian, Croatian, but not new Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to put it frankly, I don't really remember. There isn't much of a difference there any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were talking to them, they had a laptop and they were writing down what you said on to the laptop, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were noting down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't think they were writing down things about your family or your experiences in Belgium when they were interviewing you about events in Bosanski Samac, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They asked you about what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They asked you what happened to you during the war, didn't they? They asked you about Dr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They asked you about Mr. Milan Simic, they asked you about Mr. Zaric and they asked you about Mr. Tadic and they asked you about Mr. Todorovic, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they asked you questions --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they asked you questions, they wrote down your responses when they were talking to you, one of them was typing things into the laptop, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was writing down something but it was more on a -- informational basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Informational as to the investigation they were doing conducting as to what happened in Bosanski Samac during the war, and as a result of this investigational information going -- sorry, this informational information going into the computer, they printed out a four page document, sir, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: How should I know how many pages there were? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They printed out a document and the interpreter, Ms. Martinovic, read out what was on the paper to you, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: What -- well what -- she read out, I can't now remember precisely. We were talking about it, to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, they took a comprehensive statement from you as to what happened to you during the war, read it out to you and asked you to sign it as being truthful, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that statement, sir, you said that it was on the 18th that the SDS, together with paramilitary troops, went around Samac and collected weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has nothing to do with Mr. Zaric. This has to do with the accused Blagoje Simic. The Chamber said themselves that the Prosecutor can put questions based on this statement exclusively in relation to issues concerning Mr. Simo Zaric. This is really something that is not correct, not fair, from the side of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber said it couldn't be used against Dr. Simic. That's a different concept altogether. I can ask him questions about his statement, and Your Honour has told me I can. Matters that go to Dr. Simic can't be used against him and I understand that. I certainly won't be making any submission at the end of the case that it can be. So I don't know why Mr. Vukovic keeps raising the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukovic, the Chamber has already explained it is protecting the interests of Dr. Blagoje Simic, so you can rest assured that your points have been taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said in your statement, Mr. Omeranovic, was that it was on the 18th, not the 17th, that the SDS, together with paramilitary troops, went around Samac and collected weapons from some of the people, and you said they came to my house and I showed them my JNA certificate and they called a police car. They collected all of my weapons, that's weapons, plural, and put them in the trunk of the police car. They took me to this police station and, that's the SUP, and I saw a large number of soldiers in different uniforms who were from the paramilitary units. In front of the SUP they opened the trunk and one of the soldiers started beating me when he saw the weapons. I tried to show him my certificate. That's what you said in your statement on the 27th of November, 1998. Today you said it was the 17th that it happened. Are you mistaken as to the date now that I've refreshed you with what you said in your statement four years ago?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that I was mistaken about the date but to tell you about the weapons, my sons were also members and their weapons were also handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the paramilitaries who came, took more than one weapon from your house? There were weapons plural?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: There were three weapons called spagin for the three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say in the statement that the day after the takeover, that's 16th, 17th, that's the next day, later in the morning, Simo called me and said that paramilitary units had entered the city and I should not leave the house. That's what you said in your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably yes. I cannot remember precisely if that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, go on. You wanted to add something? If you wish?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There is nothing for me to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said Simo and I hardly had any contact after this that's meaning after you were released, as I was hiding and moving from house to house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: While shelling was going on, this is what I did, but as I said, I was working at the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement, I got a message from Simo that I should have -- sorry, that I should have had enough strength as this madness would end some day. A friend of mine came and asked me to work for the Red Cross in -- in order to have easier forced labour. Later on I had to perform forced labour in the trenches. Simo paid me short visits during the night. I worked digging ditches and Simo did not have the influence to avoid me from forced labour. Anyone that was family connected to Simo Zaric had to work forced labour. That's what you said to the Prosecutor in November, 1998. Is what I've read to you true or correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did not say that he came to see me when I was digging trenches, as you put it. This is not what I said. I said that this was just an informational interview but they could write down whatever they wanted because they did not present me with these minutes in my own language, it was in English. I can't read English. Why didn't they give it to me then? They could have written down that I had done anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to be fair to the witness, one sentence was later on I had to perform forced labour in the trenches. That was one sentence. After that, another sentence is Simo paid me short visits during the night. The way the witness understood obviously that it was Simo who paid him visit while he was digging trenches so just for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just reading exactly what the statement says which the witness has already agreed he made and signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll clarify that with you. You agree that you had to --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. We will go back. I've just read to you what your signed statement says. It says a friend of mine came and asked me to work for the Red Cross in order to have easier forced labour, now, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA OMERANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is not. I said that I went out to buy cigarettes and I met this friend of mine. He asked me where I was headed and I told him that I was going to buy cigarettes, and then he asked me whether I should like to work at the Red Cross, which I immediately accepted. And this is the actual truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, perhaps we have to stop here. The Trial Chamber has some rulings to make. The witness can be led out of the courtroom. He will continue his testimony on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. On the application by the Prosecution to produce part of the statement by Kemal Bobic recorded in 1998 by the Office of the Prosecutor's investigators, whereby he stated the involvement of Naser Sejdic in his arrest, the Trial Chamber has observed that during cross-examination of Kemal Bobic, Mr. Pisarevic did put the question regarding Naser Sejdic's involvement in the arrest of Kemal Bobic to him, to Mr. Bobic, when he was giving evidence for the Prosecution. That evidence including the cross-examination of Naser Sejdic, when he came to give evidence for the Defence, is sufficient. There is no need for the Prosecution to produce that part of the statement -- that part of the statement by Mr. Kemal Bobic into evidence. On the joint Defence motion to have a military expert opinion allowed, the Trial Chamber has noted the Prosecution's response and the Trial Chamber has denied the motion. The reasons are that fact witness testimony on the conflict in the municipalities of Odzak and Bosanski Samac, the structure and operations of the JNA at the material time, the separation of forces involved in the region, is sufficient. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal on matters concerning the nature of the conflict is that in cases where it is necessary to state whether the conflict was internal or international in any region at any given period relevant to the indictment involved in the trial would depend on the evidence available in each case. The Trial Chamber will make findings on the evidence available. It does not need an expert opinion. Besides the fact witness testimony, the joint statement of admissions by the parties filed in this case also sheds some light on the same issues. Dr. Andrew Gow, a political scientist only gave a historical overview of the operation of the JNA, paramilitary groups and the VJ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is inaccurate that the Prosecution introduced three expert witnesses through Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber has a role in ensuring that parties offer testimony on equal terms, but that does not mean that the Trial Chamber should call for expert opinion even on issues that would turn on eye-witness testimony, such as the identity of the parties to the armed conflict at the time relevant to the indictment. On the application by Mr. Pantelic to withdraw Mr. Selimir Simic as a witness for Dr. Blagoje Simic, the Trial Chamber has noted the response of the Prosecution but has decided to review its ruling. Mr. Selimir Simic will not be withdrawn. The Trial Chamber considers his evidence important even though mainly cumulative. His statement -- the statement recorded under Rule 92 bis, that is D163/1, will remain on record, with paragraph 20 struck out. The witness will not give viva voce evidence. He will, however, come for cross-examination only by the Prosecution, for one hour. We shall rise and continue our proceedings on Monday.
